title: Initial Lease Measurement
description: Understand how the present value of lease payments determines the initial lease liability.
html:
Lease liability at commencement

At commencement, the lease liability is generally based on the present value of lease payments that have not yet been paid.

Initial Lease Liability = Present Value of Applicable Lease Payments

Why present value?

A dollar paid several years from now is not economically equivalent to a dollar paid today.

Therefore, future lease payments are discounted to a present value.

Simple present-value example

Assume a lease requires a single payment of $10,000 one year from today.

Assume the applicable annual discount rate is 5%.

Present Value = Future Payment ÷ (1 + Rate)
$10,000 ÷ 1.05 = $9,523.81

The present value is approximately $9,524.

Multiple payments

Real leases usually contain multiple periodic payments.

Each applicable future payment is discounted based on when it will be paid, and the present values are combined.

PV = Payment₁ ÷ (1+r)¹ + Payment₂ ÷ (1+r)² + ...

Right-of-use asset

The initial ROU asset often begins with the initial lease liability, but it is not always exactly equal to it.

Certain items can adjust the ROU asset, such as applicable payments made at or before commencement, lease incentives, and certain initial direct costs.

Don't memorize this:

ROU Asset = Lease Liability in every situation.

Instead remember:

The lease liability is based on the present value of applicable unpaid lease payments, while the initial ROU asset begins from that measurement and may require adjustments.

What comes next

After initial recognition, interest accrues on the lease liability and lease payments reduce the liability.

Finance and operating leases then differ in important aspects of subsequent expense recognition.

quiz.prompt: A lease requires a single payment of $21,000 exactly one year from today. If the applicable annual discount rate is 5%, what is the approximate present value?
